raw_response: I can't reliably rank specific olive oil brands for you, because:  1. **I don't have current market data** on which oils are "leading" or how recent harvests compare. Olive oil quality varies significantly year to year, even from the same producer.  2. **"Best" depends on your use case** — finishing oil for salads and bread is different from everyday cooking oil.  3. **The olive oil market has well-documented fraud issues**, so brand reputation alone isn't reliable.  Here's a more useful framework for choosing one yourself:  **What to look for on the label:** - **Harvest date** (not just "best by") — ideally within the last 12 months - **Single origin** — one country, ideally one estate or region - **Extra virgin** + a quality seal: California Olive Oil Council (COOC), UNAPROL, DOP/PDO, or Australian Olive Association - **Dark glass or tin** — light degrades oil - **Polyphenol content** if listed (higher = more peppery, more antioxidants)  **Avoid:** - Vague "Product of [multiple countries]" blends - Clear bottles on a warm shelf - Oils without a harvest date - Suspiciously cheap "Italian" oil (often blended from elsewhere)  **Reputable categories to explore:** - California producers (strict standards, fresh): e.g., from COOC-certified estates - Australian producers (also strict, southern hemisphere harvest = fresher in spring/summer) - Greek, Spanish, or southern Italian DOP/PDO oils from a specific estate - Tunisian and Portuguese oils (often excellent value)  **Quick test at home:** Good EVOO smells grassy, fruity, or like fresh herbs/tomato leaves. It should have some peppery bite at the back of the throat (that's the polyphenols). If it tastes flat or greasy, it's past its prime or low quality.
